title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
hook: the sun, a king, his son, and a teaching handed down until it was lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as lokasangraha: King Janaka working his way to perfection, and action done to hold the world together. Who might have learned something from how you worked? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

The sun. Manu. Ikshvaku. Three names, at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action he's been explaining, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu. Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, Krishna says, over a long stretch of time, it was lost. That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield. Today, a teaching with a family tree.
screen: `THE SUN, MANU, IKSHVAKU.` → `HANDED ON, KING TO KING.` → `LOST, AND TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The Gita has a word for this handing on: parampara, one after another, teacher to student. It's how the yoga of action is said to have reached Arjuna. And Krishna tells him why it's coming to him in particular: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret. Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago. How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter. Many births have passed, he says, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't. Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and the Lord of all beings, he says he comes into being through his own power, his own maya. And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. Here's the link to our word. In the next verse, Krishna speaks of his birth and his action, his karma, as divine. Whoever truly knows them, he says, isn't born again when they leave the body, but comes to him. So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting, taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently. Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, his power, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will and not forced on him by karma, as ours are. Both are reading the same verse. And the shape of the chapter holds either way: the teaching of action comes down a chain of people, and it's renewed by one who acts.
screen: `PARAMPARA: ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES, I COME.` · `HIS BIRTH AND KARMA ARE DIVINE.` · then, large: `RENEWED BY ONE WHO ACTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one thing you know how to do that someone taught you: a recipe, a prayer, a way of tying a knot, how to apologize. Picture the person who taught you. Then, if you can, the person who taught them. Let the chain go back as far as you can see, and then a little further, into people you'll never know. Sit with the whole line behind one small skill. If you pray, you can give thanks for the whole chain. The bell holds the time.
Karma. In chapter four, a yoga of action handed down teacher to student, lost, and told again by one whose own birth and action are divine.

Your line: karma, the Gita's chapters three, four and five, re-read with commentary. Today, pass one small thing on: show someone how you do it, the way it was shown to you. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

myth: Krishna says the yoga of action is new, taught for the first time to Arjuna
he says he taught it to the sun, it was handed down, then lost, and he's telling it again.
Arjuna objects that Krishna was born after the sun
and Krishna answers that many births have passed, for both of them.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. your friend says he taught this yoga to the sun, long ago. what do you say?
options: that's impossible. you were born recently, and the sun long ago.
nothing. it's not polite to question a teacher.
fork.reveal: Arjuna objects. Krishna answers: many births have passed for me and for you; I know them all, you don't.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: parampara, one after another, the chain of teachers. Gita 4.2.

trapdoor: what you thought: an avatar is a god in disguise.
what it means: in chapter four, Krishna says that though unborn, he comes into being by his own power whenever dharma declines, and his birth and karma are divine.
what a scholar hears: the phrase 'by my own maya' in 4.6, which Shankara reads as an appearance by the Lord's power and Ramanuja as a real birth freely chosen, not bound by karma.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.1–4.3 (Vivasvan, Manu, Ikshvaku; parampara; the teaching lost and told again)
Bhagavad Gita 4.4–4.9 (Arjuna's objection; many births; 'by my own maya'; whenever dharma declines; divine birth and action)

notes: Shankara on 4.6: the Lord, by his own maya, appears to be born and embodied; Ramanuja on 4.5–6: the Lord's births are real, by his own will (atma-sankalpa), and his body is not made of karma-bound matter. Both compressed; confirm fairness.
Editor pass: 'both would agree on the shape of the chapter' (an unsourced claim about Shankara and Ramanuja) became 'the shape of the chapter holds either way'.
4.3 'my devotee and my friend' and 'this is a supreme secret': confirm paraphrase.
This day avoids 'avatar' in the voice, since the Gita here uses verbs of coming into being and sending forth; the trapdoor names it as the common term.
